Data-hungry machine learning methods have become a new standard to efficiently navigate chem-
ical compound space for molecular and materials design and discovery. Due to the severe scarcity
and cost of high-quality experimental or synthetic simulated training data, however, data-acquisition
costs can be considerable. Relying on reasonably accurate approximate legacy baseline labels with
low computational complexity represents one of the most effective strategies to curb data-needs,
e.g. through ∆-, transfer-, or multi-fidelity learning. A surprisingly effective and data-efficient base-
line model is presented in the form of a generic coarse-graining Hammett-Inspired Product (HIP)

methods.value: The HIP model generalizes the empirical Hammett equation towards arbitrary systems and properties, using a product of two scalars to predict chemical properties.

problems.value: Data-hungry machine learning methods have limitations due to the scarcity and cost of high-quality experimental or synthetic simulated training data in chemical compound space exploration.

hypotheses.value: A Hammett-Inspired Product (HIP) model can serve as a reasonably accurate and data-efficient baseline for ∆-machine learning models to curb data-needs.

evidence.value: Numerical evidence includes solvation free energies, formation energies of crystals, carbon adsorption energies, HOMO-LUMO gaps, activation energies for reactions, and catalyst-substrate binding energies.

conclusions.value: The HIP model demonstrates broad applicability and data-efficiency across chemically diverse systems, providing a fast and interpretable baseline for exploring chemical compound space.

materials.value: Numerical evidence includes solvation free energies, formation energies of crystals, carbon adsorption energies, HOMO-LUMO gaps, activation energies for reactions, and catalyst-substrate binding energies.
